topics.name: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor, an Inductor, and a Capacitor: Phasors and Reactance
topics.summary: When a sinusoidal voltage \( v=V_0\sin\omega t \) is applied to a single ideal element, the current is also sinusoidal at the same frequency, but its phase depends on the element. In a resistor, voltage and current are exactly in phase. In an inductor, voltage leads current by \( 90^\circ \); in a capacitor, current leads voltage by \( 90^\circ \) — remembered as 'ELI the ICE man'. Inductors and capacitors oppose AC through reactance: \( X_L=\omega L \) grows with frequency, while \( X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \) falls with frequency, so a capacitor blocks DC completely and an inductor passes it freely. Because the plain average of a full sine wave is zero, AC is described by RMS values, \( I_{rms}=\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2} \) and \( V_{rms}=\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2} \), which give the same heating as an equal steady DC. Mains ratings and AC meters always quote RMS values. Phasors — rotating arrows whose projections give the instantaneous values — show these phase relationships at a glance and set up the analysis of combined circuits.
topics.worked_example:
A \( 100 \) \( \mu \)F capacitor is connected to \( 200 \) V (RMS) at \( \omega=100 \) rad/s.

\( X_C=\dfrac{1}{100\times10^{-4}}=100 \) Ω.

\( I_{rms}=\dfrac{200}{100}=2 \) A, leading the voltage by \( 90^\circ \).
common_mistakes: Using a factor of \( 2 \) instead of \( \sqrt2 \) between peak and RMS values
Plugging peak values into heating or power formulas
Taking the plain average of AC (zero) when the RMS value is needed
Swapping which of V or I leads in an inductor or a capacitor
Swapping the frequency trends of \( X_L \) and \( X_C \)

topics.name: AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit: Impedance and Phase Angle
topics.summary: In a series LCR circuit the same current flows through every element, so the current phasor is the natural reference. The resistor's voltage \( V_R \) is in phase with the current, \( V_L \) leads it by \( 90^\circ \) and \( V_C \) lags it by \( 90^\circ \). Since \( V_L \) and \( V_C \) point in opposite directions, they partly cancel, and the net reactive voltage \( V_L-V_C \) is perpendicular to \( V_R \). The supply voltage is therefore the hypotenuse of a right triangle, not a plain sum. Dividing every side by the current gives the impedance triangle: \( Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2} \) and \( \tan\phi=\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R} \). When \( X_L>X_C \) the circuit is inductive and \( \phi \) is positive (voltage leads); when \( X_C>X_L \) it is capacitive and \( \phi \) is negative (current leads). Individual element voltages can exceed the supply voltage because of this vector addition. The RMS current is \( I=\dfrac{V}{Z} \), and each element voltage is \( I \) times its own resistance or reactance.
topics.worked_example:
\( R=30 \) Ω, \( X_L=80 \) Ω, \( X_C=40 \) Ω on \( 100 \) V (RMS).

\( Z=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=50 \) Ω, so \( I=2 \) A.

\( \tan\phi=\dfrac{40}{30} \), positive: the circuit is inductive and voltage leads.
common_mistakes: Adding \( R \), \( X_L \), \( X_C \) as a plain sum instead of combining them vectorially
Adding voltmeter readings directly to get the supply voltage
Dropping the sign of \( \phi \) for a capacitive circuit
Inverting the ratio in \( \tan\phi \)
Assuming no element voltage can exceed the supply

topics.name: Resonance in a Series LCR Circuit and Quality Factor
topics.summary: As the driving frequency of a series LCR circuit changes, \( X_L \) rises and \( X_C \) falls. At exactly one frequency they are equal; this is resonance. There the reactances cancel, the impedance drops to its minimum value \( Z=R \), the current reaches its maximum \( \dfrac{V}{R} \), and voltage and current are in phase (\( \phi=0 \)). Setting \( \omega L=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \) gives \( \omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \), which depends only on \( L \) and \( C \), never on \( R \). Below resonance the circuit is capacitive; above it, inductive. At resonance \( V_L \) and \( V_C \) are equal and opposite and can each be many times the supply voltage. The sharpness of the resonance peak is measured by the quality factor \( Q=\dfrac{\omega_0L}{R}=\dfrac{1}{\omega_0RC}=\dfrac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega} \), where \( \Delta\omega \) is the bandwidth between the half-power points. A smaller \( R \) gives a larger \( Q \) and a sharper, narrower peak; this is what lets a radio tuning circuit pick out one station from many.
common_mistakes: Making \( \omega_0 \) depend on \( R \)
Forgetting the square root in \( \omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \)
Thinking impedance is zero or maximum at resonance
Linking a sharper resonance to larger \( R \)
Adding \( V_L \) and \( V_C \) at resonance instead of cancelling them

topics.name: Power in AC Circuits: Average Power, Power Factor, and Wattless Current
topics.summary: Instantaneous power \( vi \) in an AC circuit changes throughout each cycle, so what matters is its average. Only the part of the current in phase with the voltage delivers net energy, giving \( P=V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\phi \), where \( \cos\phi \) is the power factor. In a series circuit \( \cos\phi=\dfrac{R}{Z} \), and the power is also simply \( I_{rms}^2R \), because only the resistor turns electrical energy into heat. For a pure resistor \( \cos\phi=1 \); at resonance it is also \( 1 \). For a pure inductor or capacitor \( \phi=90^\circ \), so \( \cos\phi=0 \) and the average power is zero: energy stored in one quarter-cycle is returned in the next. The current in such a circuit is real and measurable but does no net work; it is called wattless current. This is why a choke coil, not a resistor, is used to limit current in lamp circuits, and why industries add capacitors to raise a low power factor. Always use RMS values, never peak values, in these formulas.
common_mistakes: Dropping \( \cos\phi \) and using \( V_{rms}I_{rms} \) as the power
Using peak values in the power formula
Claiming a pure inductor or capacitor dissipates \( I^2X \)
Thinking wattless current means no current flows
Treating power factor as always \( 1 \)

topics.name: LC Oscillations and the Transformer
topics.summary: When a charged capacitor is connected across an ideal inductor, charge flows back and forth and energy shuttles between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field. When the capacitor is fully charged the current is zero; when it is fully discharged the current is maximum. This is exactly like a spring-mass system: charge corresponds to displacement, current to velocity, \( L \) to mass and \( \dfrac{1}{C} \) to the spring constant. The oscillation has \( \omega=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \) and period \( T=2\pi\sqrt{LC} \), and with no resistance the total energy stays constant; any resistance damps it, like friction. The transformer uses mutual induction: an alternating primary current creates a changing flux that induces an emf in the secondary, so it works only with AC. For an ideal transformer \( \dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} \), while power conservation \( V_pI_p=V_sI_s \) makes the current ratio the inverse, \( \dfrac{I_s}{I_p}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s} \). Stepping up voltage steps down current, which cuts \( I^2R \) losses in power transmission.
topics.worked_example:
An ideal transformer with \( N_p:N_s=10:1 \) has \( 2200 \) V on the primary and an \( 11 \) Ω load.

\( V_s=220 \) V, \( I_s=20 \) A.

\( I_p=\dfrac{20}{10}=2 \) A; power \( 4400 \) W on both sides.
common_mistakes: Applying the turns ratio to current in the same direction as voltage
Thinking a transformer changes power, or works on DC
Halving the charge instead of the energy when energy is shared equally
Swapping the analogues: \( L \) is mass, \( \dfrac{1}{C} \) is the spring constant
Forgetting \( 2\pi \) or the square root in \( T=2\pi\sqrt{LC} \)

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor, an Inductor, and a Capacitor: Phasors and Reactance
questions.question: In an AC circuit containing only a resistor, what is the phase relationship between the voltage across it and the current through it?
questions.explanation:
For a resistor, \( v=Ri \) holds at every instant.

With \( v=V_0\sin\omega t \), the current is \( i=\dfrac{V_0}{R}\sin\omega t \), the same sine function.

So voltage and current are exactly in phase, \( \phi=0 \).
questions.hint: Ohm's law \( v=Ri \) applies at every instant, not just on average.
distractor_logic: This is the pure-inductor behaviour, not the resistor's
This is the pure-capacitor behaviour, not the resistor's
Imagines the resistor opposing the voltage; Ohm's law makes \( v \) and \( i \) rise and fall together

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor, an Inductor, and a Capacitor: Phasors and Reactance
questions.question: For an ideal inductor connected to an AC source, which statement about phase is correct?
options: Voltage and current are in phase
questions.explanation:
The inductor's back-emf opposes changes in current, so the current builds up a quarter-cycle after the voltage.

Mathematically, \( v=V_0\sin\omega t \) gives \( i=I_0\sin\left(\omega t-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \).

So voltage leads current by \( 90^\circ \) — 'ELI': E (voltage) before I in L.
questions.hint: Remember 'ELI the ICE man' — in L, E comes before I.
distractor_logic: Swaps the ELI rule; current leading is the capacitor (ICE) case
That is true only for a pure resistor
\( 45^\circ \) needs a resistor with \( R=X_L \); a pure inductor gives a full \( 90^\circ \)

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor, an Inductor, and a Capacitor: Phasors and Reactance
questions.question: For an ideal capacitor connected to an AC source, which statement about phase is correct?
options: Current and voltage are in phase
questions.explanation:
Current must flow onto the capacitor before its charge, and hence its voltage, can build up.

With \( v=V_0\sin\omega t \), \( i=C\dfrac{dv}{dt}=I_0\sin\left(\omega t+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \).

So current leads voltage by \( 90^\circ \) — 'ICE': I before E in C.
questions.hint: Remember 'ELI the ICE man' — in C, I comes before E.
distractor_logic: Swaps the ICE rule; voltage leading is the inductor (ELI) case
That is true only for a pure resistor
No single ideal element produces a \( 180^\circ \) shift between its own \( v \) and \( i \)

questions.question: An inductor of \( 0.5 \) H is connected to an AC source of angular frequency \( \omega=100 \) rad/s. What is its inductive reactance?
questions.explanation:
Inductive reactance is \( X_L=\omega L \).

\( X_L=100\times0.5=50 \) Ω.
questions.hint: Inductive reactance grows directly with both \( \omega \) and \( L \).
distractor_logic: Divided \( L \) by \( \omega \) instead of multiplying
Used the capacitor-style form \( \dfrac{1}{\omega L} \)
Computed \( \dfrac{\omega}{L} \) instead of \( \omega L \)

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor, an Inductor, and a Capacitor: Phasors and Reactance
questions.question: As the frequency of the AC source across a capacitor is increased, its capacitive reactance \( X_C \):
options: Increases, because \( X_C \) is proportional to \( \omega \)
Stays constant, since it depends only on \( C \)
questions.explanation:
Capacitive reactance is \( X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \).

\( \omega \) sits in the denominator, so raising the frequency lowers \( X_C \).

Physically, at high frequency the capacitor has little time to charge up, so it opposes the current less.
questions.hint: Look at where \( \omega \) sits in the formula for \( X_C \).
distractor_logic: Swaps the frequency trend of \( X_C \) with that of \( X_L \)
Forgets that \( \omega \) appears in the reactance formula
Invents a peak; \( X_C \) falls steadily as \( \omega \) rises

questions.question: An AC current has a peak value \( I_0=10\sqrt2 \) A. What is its RMS value?
questions.explanation:
For a sinusoid, \( I_{rms}=\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2} \).

\( I_{rms}=\dfrac{10\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}=10 \) A.
questions.hint: The RMS value of a sinusoid is its peak divided by \( \sqrt2 \), not by \( 2 \).
distractor_logic: Quoted the peak value as the RMS value
Divided the peak by \( 2 \) instead of \( \sqrt2 \)
Multiplied by \( \sqrt2 \) instead of dividing

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor, an Inductor, and a Capacitor: Phasors and Reactance
questions.question: What is the simple time-average of the current \( i=I_0\sin\omega t \) taken over one complete cycle?
questions.explanation:
Over a full cycle the positive half and the negative half of the sine wave are identical in size.

They cancel, so the plain average is exactly zero.

This is precisely why the RMS value is used as the meaningful 'effective' value of AC.
questions.hint: Compare the area of the positive half-cycle with the negative half-cycle.
distractor_logic: That is the RMS value, not the plain average
Guesses a half-peak average; the positive and negative halves cancel exactly
Confuses the peak with the average

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Resistor, an Inductor, and a Capacitor: Phasors and Reactance
questions.question: What is the reactance offered by an ideal capacitor to a steady DC voltage (\( \omega=0 \))?
options: Zero, so it behaves like a plain wire
The same as at any AC frequency
Infinite, so no steady current flows
questions.explanation:
\( X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \).

For DC, \( \omega=0 \), so \( X_C \) becomes infinitely large.

Once charged, the capacitor blocks steady DC completely.
questions.hint: Put \( \omega=0 \) into \( X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \).
distractor_logic: This is the inductor's behaviour on DC, not the capacitor's
Dropped \( \omega \) from \( X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \), effectively taking \( \omega=1 \)
Ignores that \( X_C \) depends on frequency

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit: Impedance and Phase Angle
questions.question: Which expression gives the impedance of a series LCR circuit?
questions.explanation:
\( V_R \) is along the current; \( V_L \) and \( V_C \) are perpendicular to it and opposite to each other.

Net reactive voltage is \( I(X_L-X_C) \), at right angles to \( IR \).

Pythagoras gives \( Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2} \).
questions.hint: Think of a right triangle with \( R \) along one side.
distractor_logic: Adds all three as a plain sum, ignoring their phase differences
Squares each separately, ignoring that \( X_L \) and \( X_C \) oppose each other
Combines algebraically instead of as perpendicular phasors

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit: Impedance and Phase Angle
questions.question: In a series LCR circuit, the phase angle \( \phi \) between voltage and current is given by:
questions.explanation:
In the impedance triangle, \( R \) is the adjacent side and \( X_L-X_C \) is the opposite side.

So \( \tan\phi=\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R} \).
questions.hint: Opposite side over adjacent side in the impedance triangle.
distractor_logic: Inverted the ratio in the impedance triangle
Added the reactances although they oppose each other
That ratio is \( \sin\phi \), not \( \tan\phi \)

questions.explanation:

A positive \( \phi \) means the circuit behaves inductively and voltage leads current.

questions.question: In a series RC circuit on AC, how does the current compare in phase with the supply voltage?
options: Current lags voltage by an angle between \( 0^\circ \) and \( 90^\circ \)
Current leads voltage by an angle between \( 0^\circ \) and \( 90^\circ \)
Current and voltage are in phase
questions.explanation:
The capacitor pulls the current ahead of the voltage, while the resistor keeps them in step.

The combination gives \( \phi \) negative with magnitude between \( 0^\circ \) and \( 90^\circ \): current leads by less than \( 90^\circ \).
questions.hint: It sits between the pure-R and pure-C extremes.

questions.question: In a series RL circuit, voltmeters read \( 30 \) V across the resistor and \( 40 \) V across the inductor. What is the supply voltage?
questions.explanation:
\( V_R \) and \( V_L \) are \( 90^\circ \) apart.

\( V=\sqrt{V_R^2+V_L^2}=\sqrt{900+1600}=50 \) V.
questions.hint: The two voltages are perpendicular phasors.

questions.topic: AC Voltage Applied to a Series LCR Circuit: Impedance and Phase Angle
questions.question: In a series LCR circuit, which quantity is the same for all three elements at every instant?
questions.explanation:
In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same current flows through \( R \), \( L \) and \( C \) at every instant.

That is why the current phasor is used as the reference in LCR phasor diagrams.
questions.hint: There is only one path for charge in a series circuit.
distractor_logic: Equal voltage is a property of parallel elements, not series
Each element's voltage has a different phase relative to the current
The resistor has no reactance, and \( X_L \), \( X_C \) generally differ

questions.topic: Resonance in a Series LCR Circuit and Quality Factor
questions.question: What is the condition for resonance in a series LCR circuit?
questions.explanation:
At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel exactly: \( X_L=X_C \).

Then \( Z=R \) and the circuit is purely resistive.
questions.hint: What makes the reactive part of \( Z \) vanish?
distractor_logic: Confuses resonance with the \( 45^\circ \) condition
Invents a factor; the reactances must cancel exactly
Resonance does not require zero resistance

questions.topic: Resonance in a Series LCR Circuit and Quality Factor
questions.question: The resonant angular frequency of a series LCR circuit is:
questions.explanation:
Set \( \omega_0L=\dfrac{1}{\omega_0C} \).

Then \( \omega_0^2=\dfrac{1}{LC} \), so \( \omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \).

\( R \) does not appear.
questions.hint: Equate \( X_L \) and \( X_C \) and solve for \( \omega \).
distractor_logic: Forgot the square root
Inverted the expression
Made \( \omega_0 \) depend on \( R \); it depends only on \( L \) and \( C \)

questions.topic: Resonance in a Series LCR Circuit and Quality Factor
questions.question: At resonance, the impedance of a series LCR circuit is:
options: Equal to \( R \), its minimum possible value
questions.explanation:
With \( X_L=X_C \), \( Z=\sqrt{R^2+0}=R \).

Since \( (X_L-X_C)^2\geq0 \) always, \( Z \) can never be smaller than \( R \), so this is the minimum.
questions.hint: Put \( X_L-X_C=0 \) in the impedance formula.
distractor_logic: Only the reactances cancel; \( R \) remains
Series resonance minimises \( Z \); a plain sum is never correct
Forgets that \( X_L \) is cancelled by \( X_C \)

questions.topic: Resonance in a Series LCR Circuit and Quality Factor
questions.question: What is the phase angle \( \phi \) between voltage and current in a series LCR circuit at resonance?
questions.explanation:
At resonance \( \tan\phi=\dfrac{X_L-X_C}{R}=0 \).

So \( \phi=0 \): voltage and current are in phase.
questions.hint: At resonance the circuit behaves like a pure resistor.
distractor_logic: That is the pure-inductor value
That is the pure-capacitor value
That occurs when \( |X_L-X_C|=R \), at the half-power points

questions.question: The quality factor \( Q \) of a series LCR circuit is defined as:
questions.explanation:
\( Q=\dfrac{\omega_0L}{R}=\dfrac{1}{\omega_0RC}=\dfrac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega} \).

It compares the reactance at resonance with the resistance, and is dimensionless.

questions.explanation:

questions.explanation:

questions.question: An ideal \( 1:2 \) step-up transformer is fed with \( 220 \) V (RMS) mains. What is the peak voltage on its secondary?
questions.explanation:
\( V_{s,rms}=2\times220=440 \) V.

Peak \( =\sqrt2\times440=440\sqrt2 \) V.
questions.hint: Apply the turns ratio, then convert RMS to peak.

Converted to peak but ignored the turns ratio
Used a factor of \( 2 \) instead of \( \sqrt2 \) for the peak

questions.question: A series LCR circuit with \( R=10 \) Ω and \( Q=5 \) is at resonance on a \( 20 \) V (RMS) supply. What is the RMS voltage across the capacitor?
questions.explanation:
At resonance \( I=\dfrac{20}{10}=2 \) A and \( X_C=\omega_0L=QR=50 \) Ω.

\( V_C=2\times50=100 \) V \( =Q\times V \).
questions.hint: At resonance \( V_C=V_L=QV \).
distractor_logic: Assumed no element exceeds the supply voltage
Divided the supply by \( Q \)
Confused the capacitor alone with the L-C pair

questions.question: A series LCR circuit with \( R=50 \) Ω on a \( 200 \) V (RMS) supply is driven off resonance, where \( |X_L-X_C|=50\sqrt3 \) Ω. What are the current and the phase magnitude?
questions.explanation:
\( Z=\sqrt{2500+7500}=100 \) Ω, so \( I=2 \) A (half the resonant \( 4 \) A).

\( \tan|\phi|=\sqrt3 \), so \( |\phi|=60^\circ \).

questions.question: Setting \( X_L=X_C \) gives the resonance condition. Which form is equivalent?
questions.explanation:
\( \omega L=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \).

Multiply by \( \omega C \): \( \omega^2LC=1 \).
questions.hint: Cross-multiply \( \omega L=\dfrac{1}{\omega C} \).

Brought \( R \) into the resonance condition

questions.question: At a half-power frequency of a series LCR circuit, which is correct?
questions.explanation:
Half power: \( I^2=\dfrac{I_{max}^2}{2} \), so \( Z=\sqrt2R \).

\( |X_L-X_C|=R \), \( |\phi|=45^\circ \), \( \cos\phi=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \).
questions.hint: Power \( \propto I^2 \), so current drops by \( \sqrt2 \).
distractor_logic: Zero power factor means zero power, not half
Thinks half power means a power factor of one-half
That is resonance, the maximum-power point

questions.question: In an ideal LC circuit (no resistance), which quantity stays constant during the oscillations?
options: The total energy, but it decreases a little every cycle
The total energy, doubling every half cycle
The total energy, which is zero whenever \( i=0 \)
questions.explanation:
Neither ideal L nor ideal C dissipates power (both have \( \cos\phi=0 \)).

So the total energy \( \dfrac{q^2}{2C}+\dfrac{1}{2}Li^2 \) is conserved.
questions.hint: Which element could dissipate energy?
distractor_logic: Only a resistor dissipates energy; there is none here
Energy cannot grow without a source
When \( i=0 \) all the energy is in the capacitor

questions.question: An ideal transformer's primary is connected to AC with the secondary open (no load). How does the primary current relate to the voltage?
options: It lags the voltage by nearly \( 90^\circ \), so almost no power is drawn
It is in phase, drawing the full \( V_{rms}I_{rms} \)
questions.explanation:
With no load, the primary behaves as a nearly pure inductor.

Current lags by about \( 90^\circ \), \( \cos\phi\approx0 \): a wattless current.
questions.hint: What element is an unloaded primary coil?
distractor_logic: The primary is an inductor: ELI, not ICE
Treats the primary as a resistor
A small magnetising current still flows
